# Chapter 1
# Set 1
Q1: What does Jagan say one must do to conquer the self?
A) Meditate daily
B) Conquer taste
C) Reject material possessions
D) Follow a guru
Answer: B
Ex- Jagan states, "Conquer taste and you will have conquered the self."
Q2: Who is Jagan talking to in the beginning of the chapter?
A) His son
B) His wife
C) A cousin
D) A customer
Answer: C
Ex- The listener is referred to as a cousin, though the exact relation is unclear.
Q3: What does Jagan place on the picture frame of the goddess Lakshmi?
A) A garland of roses
B) A string of jasmine
C) A marigold wreath
D) A lotus flower
Answer: B
Ex- Jagan places a string of jasmine on top of the picture frame.
Q4: Where does Jagan's cousin go first when he visits?
A) The prayer room
B) Jagan's office
C) The kitchen
D) The veranda
Answer: C
Ex- The cousin passes straight into the kitchen when he arrives.
Q5: What does Jagan's cousin say about the sugar situation?
A) The price may increase
B) There is a shortage
C) The quality has improved
D) The government is lowering the price
Answer: A
Ex- The cousin mentions that the government may raise the price of sugar.
Q6: How often does Jagan shave?
A) Daily
B) Every other day
C) Once a week
D) At certain intervals
Answer: D
Ex- Jagan shaves only at certain intervals, finding daily shaving an intolerable European habit.
Q7: What material are Jagan's clothes made from?
A) Cotton
B) Silk
C) Wool
D) Material he spins himself
Answer: D
Ex- Jagan wears clothes made from material he spins with his own hand.
Q8: How much cash does Jagan earn monthly from spinning?
A) Less than five rupees
B) Around ten rupees
C) More than twenty rupees
D) He doesn't sell the excess yarn
Answer: A
Ex- Jagan earns less than five rupees a month from selling excess yarn to the local hand-loom committee.
Q9: When did Jagan begin the habit of spinning?
A) In his childhood
B) After getting married
C) When Gandhi visited the town
D) After retiring from work
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan began spinning when Gandhi visited the town over twenty years ago.
Q10: What is Jagan's footwear made from?
A) Leather from an animal that died naturally
B) Synthetic materials
C) Cloth spun by himself
D) Rubber soles
Answer: A
Ex- Jagan wears sandals made from the leather of an animal which died of old age.
Q11: Who helps Jagan tan the leather for his footwear?
A) His wife
B) His son
C) An old cobbler
D) He does it himself
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan turns the leather over to an old cobbler who has a repair-shop under a tree.
Q12: How did Jagan's wife react to his leather tanning?
A) She helped him enthusiastically
B) She tolerated it reluctantly
C) She shut herself in a room in protest
D) She threw away the leather
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan's wife shut herself in a room and refused to come out until the tanning ended.
Q13: What did Jagan's wife possibly say on her deathbed?
A) "I love you"
B) "Take care of our son"
C) "Throw away the leather"
D) "Forgive me"
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan thought his wife was probably saying "Throw away the leather" with her last words.
Q14: What did Jagan do with the last bit of leather after his wife's death?
A) Buried it with her
B) Gave it to his son
C) Donated it to a mission
D) Kept it as a memento
Answer: C
Ex- In deference to his wife's possible last wish, Jagan gave the last bit of leather to a mission.
Q15: What has Jagan given up since morning?
A) Wheat
B) Honey
C) Rice
D) Salt
Answer: D
Ex- Jagan announces that he has given up salt since that morning.
Q16: According to Jagan, what should one eat instead of regular salt?
A) Sea salt
B) Rock salt
C) Natural salt
D) No salt at all
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan expands his theory, stating "One must eat only natural salt."
Q17: What does the cousin jokingly suggest natural salt could be?
A) Salt from the Dead Sea
B) Salt obtained from seawater
C) Salt that dries up on one's back after running in the sun
D) Salt found in natural salt mines
Answer: C
Ex- The cousin jokes that natural salt could be "the salt that dries up on one's back when one has run a mile in the sun".
Q18: How does Jagan react to the cousin's joke about natural salt?
A) He laughs heartily
B) He ignores the comment
C) He makes a wry face
D) He changes the subject
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan makes a wry face at the cousin's coarse reference.
Q19: What European habit does Jagan find intolerable?
A) Wearing suits
B) Eating with a fork and knife
C) Drinking tea
D) Viewing oneself daily in a mirror
Answer: D
Ex- Jagan feels that viewing oneself daily in a mirror is an intolerable European habit.
Q20: What has Jagan discontinued in addition to salt?
A) Honey
B) Wheat
C) Sugar
D) Greens
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan mentions that the cousin knows he has discontinued sugar.
Q21: How many drops of honey does Jagan find adequate?
A) Five
B) Ten
C) Twenty
D) Thirty
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan finds twenty drops of honey in hot water quite adequate.
Q22: What does Jagan cook and take with honey and greens?
A) Rice
B) Stone-ground wheat
C) Oats
D) Barley
Answer: B
Ex- Jagan cooks a little stone-ground wheat and takes it with honey and greens.
Q23: According to the cousin, what art has Jagan perfected?
A) The art of cooking
B) The art of living on nothing
C) The art of spinning
D) The art of tanning leather
Answer: B
Ex- The cousin says, "You have perfected the art of living on nothing."
Q24: Who was the cousin talking to about Jagan's self-dependence?
A) The Tax Collector
B) The Cooperative Registrar
C) The Police Commissioner
D) The Bank Manager
Answer: B
Ex- The cousin mentions he was speaking to the Cooperative Registrar about how Jagan has simplified his life.
Q25: What is Jagan's overall outlook on life?
A) Materialistic and worldly
B) Cynical and pessimistic
C) Carefree and joyful
D) Disembodied and detached from earthly grime
Answer: D
Ex- Jagan is described as having the outlook of a disembodied soul floating above the grime of this earth.
# Set 2
Q1: What time does Jagan's counting hour approach?
A) Four o'clock
B) Five o'clock
C) Six o'clock
D) Seven o'clock
Answer: C
Ex- The text states that the time was six, when Jagan's counting hour was approaching.
Q2: How old is Jagan's wooden chair?
A) Nearly a decade old
B) Nearly half a century old
C) Nearly a century old
D) Nearly two centuries old
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan's wooden chair is described as being nearly a century old.
Q3: Why was the wooden chair specially made by Jagan's father?
A) For family gatherings
B) For an Englishman who visited for astrology lessons
C) As a wedding gift for Jagan
D) As a display piece for the shop
Answer: B
Ex- The chair was made for Mr. Noble, an Englishman who visited for astrology lessons and found it painful to sit on the floor.
Q4: What happened to Mr. Noble's signed portrait?
A) It was framed and hung in the shop
B) It was lost during a house move
C) The children played with it and it ended up in the loft
D) Jagan kept it in his desk drawer
Answer: C
Ex- The children played with Mr. Noble's portrait, substituted it with a picture of a God, and the photograph ended up in the loft.
Q5: What book does Jagan read while sitting on his chair?
A) The Ramayana
B) The Upanishads
C) The Bhagavad Gita
D) The Vedas
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan's gaze is fixed on the Sanskrit lines in a red-bound copy of the Bhagavad Gita.
Q6: What does Jagan do if he notices a pause in the kitchen's sizzling noise?
A) He ignores it and continues reading
B) He sends the head cook to check
C) He cries out, "What is happening?"
D) He goes to the kitchen himself
Answer: C
Ex- If there is the slightest pause in the sizzling, Jagan cries out, "What is happening?" without lifting his eyes from the sacred text.
Q7: Who is "Captain"?
A) The head cook
B) The front-stall boy
C) The watchman at the door
D) Jagan's son
Answer: C
Ex- When Jagan shouts "Captain!", it alerts the watchman at the door, an ex-army man in khaki.
Q8: When is the beggar allowed to be seen at the shop?
A) Mondays
B) Wednesdays
C) Fridays
D) Sundays
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan says, "Captain, that beggar should not be seen here except on Fridays."
Q9: Where does the front-stall boy drop the cash he receives?
A) In a cashbox
B) In a long-necked bronze jug
C) Directly in Jagan's hands
D) In a safe under the counter
Answer: B
Ex- The front-stall boy drops every paisa he receives into a long-necked bronze jug.
Q10: When are the shutters of the shop drawn?
A) Five o'clock
B) Six o'clock
C) Seven o'clock
D) Eight o'clock
Answer: C
Ex- The front-stall boy brings in another instalment of cash in a smaller container at seven, when the shutters are drawn.
Q11: What question does Jagan routinely ask when his staff assembles at his desk?
A) "How much did we earn today?"
B) "Is everything cleaned and put away?"
C) "How much is left over?"
D) "Did any customer complain today?"
Answer: C
Ex- When Jagan knows that all of his staff are assembled at his desk, he asks the routine question, "How much is left over?"
Q12: How much Mysore Pak is left over?
A) One seer
B) Two seers
C) Half a seer
D) Five seers
Answer: B
Ex- The staff informs Jagan that two seers of Mysore Pak are left over.
Q13: What does Jagan say about the leftover Mysore Pak?
A) "Throw it away."
B) "Distribute it among the staff."
C) "That we can sell tomorrow."
D) "Use it in a new recipe."
Answer: C
Ex- Regarding the leftover Mysore Pak, Jagan says, "That we can sell tomorrow."
Q14: How much jilebi is left over?
A) One seer
B) Two seers
C) Half a seer
D) Quarter seer
Answer: C
Ex- The staff tells Jagan that half a seer of jilebi is left over.
Q15: What does Jagan say about the leftover jilebi?
A) "It will still be good tomorrow."
B) "Won't be so good tomorrow."
C) "Fry it again for tomorrow."
D) "Give it to the watchman."
Answer: B
Ex- Regarding the leftover jilebi, Jagan says, "Won't be so good tomorrow."
Q16: What bothers Jagan's mind like a splinter under his skull?
A) The day's low sales
B) The staff's carelessness
C) The leftover sweets
D) The rising prices of ingredients
Answer: C
Ex- The leftover sweets rankle in Jagan's mind as if he has a splinter under his skull.
Q17: What does Jagan love to see at the end of the day?
A) Happy customers
B) Clean, shining trays returning to the kitchen
C) A large profit in his ledger
D) His staff working hard
Answer: B
Ex- Jagan loves to see clean, shining trays return to the kitchen at the end of a day.
Q18: What does the head cook suggest to avoid leftovers?
A) Reducing the quantity of sweets made
B) Giving discounts at the end of the day
C) Trying a new sweet the next day
D) Selling the leftovers to a nearby restaurant
Answer: C
Ex- The head cook suggests trying a new sweet the next day to avoid the problem of leftovers.
Q19: According to Jagan, what three things do sweets consist of?
A) Flour, sugar, and flavors
B) Milk, sugar, and nuts
C) Butter, flour, and syrup
D) Coconut, jaggery, and ghee
Answer: A
Ex- Jagan philosophically says, "After all, everything consists of flour, sugar, and flavours."
Q20: What is Jagan's table drawer padded with?
A) A folded towel
B) A piece of foam
C) Old newspapers
D) A velvet cloth
Answer: A
Ex- Jagan's table drawer is padded with a folded towel to muffle the sound of coins.
Q21: How long does it take Jagan to count the day's cash?
A) Five minutes
B) Ten minutes
C) Fifteen minutes
D) Twenty minutes
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan's eyes sweep the cash collection and he arrives at the final count within fifteen minutes.
Q22: Where does Jagan record the cash that comes in after six o'clock?
A) In a ledger open for inspection
B) In a small notebook
C) On a slip of paper
D) He doesn't record it separately
Answer: B
Ex- In his small notebook, Jagan enters only the cash that comes in after six o'clock, out of the smaller jug.
Q23: How does Jagan view the cash that comes in after six o'clock?
A) As a bonus
B) As a tip for good service
C) As free cash, a self-generated category
D) As a contribution to charity
Answer: C
Ex- Jagan views the cash that comes in after six as free cash, a sort of immaculate conception, self-generated.
Q24: What does Jagan do with the "free cash"?
A) Deposits it in the bank
B) Uses it for daily expenses
C) Gives it to his staff as a bonus
D) Converts it to crisp currency and stores it in the loft
Answer: D
Ex- The "free cash" is converted into crisp currency, tied into a bundle, and put away in the loft at home.
Q25: Who checks the lock on the door at the end of the day?
A) Jagan himself
B) The head cook
C) The front-stall boy
D) The watchman, referred to as "Captain"
Answer: D
Ex- Jagan asks "Captain" to see if the lock is all right, and the watchman checks it in a martial grip.

C) Film stars, cricket, and fashion
D) Their academic studies

Answer: A

A) It marked the entrance to the city
B) It was a landmark he passed by daily
C) It reminded him of the city's history
D) It held personal meaning for him
Answer: B

A) To provide medical services to the community
B) To conduct research on natural remedies
C) To train future doctors and nurses
D) To distribute government healthcare schemes
Answer: A

A) Residential developments beyond the city limits
B) Industrial zones established outside the city center
C) Commercial districts for businesses and shops
D) Public parks and recreation areas
Answer: A

A) To allow water drainage under the road
B) To provide shelter for the homeless
C) To serve as a public seating area
D) To act as a landmark for the intersection
Answer: A
The passage refers to it as "a culvert", suggesting it was an underground structure for drainage purposes.

B) He was an employee of the local municipality
C) He was waiting for food scraps from nearby homes
D) He was a threat to the safety of passersby
Answer: C

The passage states the vagrant "was waiting for: for the dining leaves to be cast out of the homes in Kabir Lane: he would collect them, scour them with his hands, and fill his belly with any vegetables and rice that might be left on them."

A) It regulated the operating hours of local shops
B) It provided tax incentives for small businesses
C) It promoted fair trade practices in the market
D) It established guidelines for street vendors
Answer: A
The passage notes that the "Truth Printing" establishment "was.shut in deference to the Shopping Hours Act", indicating it was a law regulating business hours.

A) They were part of the city's public transportation
B) They were emergency vehicles responding to a call
C) They were private cars and bicycles of local residents
D) They were commercial delivery vehicles transporting goods
Answer: C

B) They were a protected natural reserve for wildlife
C) They were where the dining leaves were gathered from
D) They were the location of Jagan's ancestral home

A) Tense and anxious

C) Optimistic and forward-looking
D) Cynical and critical

The passage depicts Jagan in a contemplative, introspective state as he walks home, reflecting on various aspects of his community and society.

A) Went straight to his bedroom
B) Switched on the light in the front room
C) Greeted his wife and son
D) Prepared himself a cup of tea
Answer: B
The passage states that Jagan "let himself into his house, switched on the light in the front room, took off his upper cloth and hung it on a nail in the wall".

A) Hung it on the wall
B) Placed it in a basket for washing
C) Folded it neatly and set it aside
D) Gave it to his wife to mend
Answer: B
The passage mentions that Jagan "took off his jibba and thrust it into a basket for tomorrow's wash".
Q3: What did Jagan do after passing through the courtyards and corridors?
A) Went to his bedroom
B) Stood gazing at the stars
C) Visited his son Mali's room
D) Checked on his wife's condition
Answer: B
The passage states that Jagan "reached the back door, lifted the cross bar, and let it down gently. He stood for a moment gazing at the stars, enthralled at the spectacle of the firmament."
Q4: What was Jagan's knowledge of astronomy limited to?
A) Identifying the major constellations
B) Determining the position of the Pole Star
C) Distinguishing between planets and stars
D) Understanding the movement of celestial bodies
Answer: B
The passage mentions that Jagan's astronomy knowledge was "limited to the location of the Pole Star from Orion's Belt or Sword or some such point".
Q5: What did Jagan call the "extraordinarily lively firework" in the sky?
A) The North Star
B) Venus or Jupiter
C) The Milky Way
D) Sirius, the Dog Star
Answer: B
The passage states that Jagan "called it sometimes Venus, sometimes Jupiter, never being sure, but admiring it unreservedly".
Q6: What was the condition of the bathroom in Jagan's house?
A) Well-maintained and modern
B) Dilapidated and in need of repair
C) Adequate but lacking in privacy
D) Spacious and comfortable
Answer: C

The passage describes the bathroom as "a shack, roofed with corrugated sheets; beaten-out tin was fixed anyhow to a wooden frame to serve as a door on rusty hinges; the wooden frame was warped and the door never shut flush bur always left a gap".
Q7: What was the practice in Jagan's house regarding the bathroom?
A) Everyone was expected to use it regularly
B) The family members avoided looking inside
C) It was only used for bathing, not other purposes
D) Guests were not allowed to use the bathroom
Answer: B
The passage states that "it had been a house practice, for generations, for its members not to look through" the gap in the bathroom door.
Q8: How did Jagan's father expand the house?
A) By building additions to the front
B) By constructing a separate wing
C) By demolishing the old hut and building from scratch
D) By gradually expanding from the back yard to the front
Answer: D
The passage explains that Jagan's father "expanded the house from the back yard to the front".
Q9: What was Jagan's father's theory about growing coconut trees?
A) They required deep watering
B) They needed constant sunlight
C) They thrived with the addition of salt
D) They were best grown in well-drained soil
Answer: C
The passage states that Jagan's father "filled the pits with great quantities of salt. 'Salt is the only thing that can make a coconut tree grow,' he remarked every day."
Q10: What was Jagan's view on using a toothbrush?
A) He preferred using a margosa twig
B) He believed toothbrushes were unhygienic
C) He thought toothbrushes were too expensive
D) He felt they could damage the tooth enamel
Answer: A

The passage mentions that Jagan "was opposed to the use of a toothbrush" and "regularly at five in the morning Jagan got up from bed, broke a twig from a matgosa tree in the back yard, chewed its tip, and brushed his teeth."
Q11: What was Jagan's view on the properties of the margosa tree?
A) It was a sacred tree that should be revered
B) It had health benefits that he strongly believed in
C) It was the only tree that could provide suitable twigs for brushing teeth
D) It had a pleasant aroma that he found soothing
Answer: B

The passage states that Jagan "had immense faith in the properties of margosa, and in spite. of its bitterness, he called it "Amrita," the ambrosia which kept the Gods alive; and sometimes he called it "Sanjeevini," the rare herb mentioned in the epics which, held at the nostrils, could bring the dead to life."
Q12: How did Jagan's wife react to his margosa-based health remedies?
A) She eagerly embraced them and followed his advice
B) She was indifferent and did not engage with his theories
C) She strongly opposed his ideas and found them impractical
D) She secretly tried the remedies without his knowledge
Answer: C
The passage describes how "His wife refused co associate herself with any of his health-giving activities. She hated his theories and lived her own life."
Q13: What happened when Jagan tried to convince his wife to use margosa flowers instead of aspirin?
A) She refused to listen to him and took the aspirin
B) She angrily rejected his suggestion and had a heated argument
C) She agreed to try the margosa remedy but found it ineffective
D) She compromised and took both the aspirin and the margosa
Answer: B

The passage recounts that "Seated beside the ancient pillar in their courtyard, she had knotted a towel around her temples and swayed madly back and forth, desperately begging for aspirin. Jagan 'was very sympathetic, no doubt, but was convinced that aspirin would do her no good. She had just-looked up at him and said, 'Oh, this headache is nor half as unbearable as your talk. You would sooner see me dead, I suppose.'"
Q14: Where did Mali have his own room in the house?
A) In the attic
B) In the front wing
C) In a hall without ventilation
D) Adjacent to his parents' room
Answer: C
The passage states that Mali "got a long hall without a ventilator or window, known 2s the 'cool room' in those days".
Q15: What did Mali have in his room?
A) A bed and a desk
B) Books and building blocks
C) A television and some toys
D) A personal computer and electronic gadgets
Answer: B
The passage mentions that Mali "had a few books heaped on the round table and some house-building blocks" in his room.
Q16: Why was Mali not allowed to touch his mother's headache pill?
A) His mother was afraid he might accidentally overdose
B) Mali had a history of misusing medication
C) The pill was kept out of reach as a safety precaution
D) The family believed traditional remedies were better
Answer: C

The passage states that Mali "had insisted upon having a room of his own, and in that vast house it was not difficult co find him one" and that "the pill" was kept "on the very top, so high that you all think I cannot reach it".
Q17: What did Jagan do after finding his wife's headache pill?
A) He immediately gave it to her
B) He hid the pill so Mali couldn't find it
C) He disposed of the pill and suggested a natural remedy
D) He lectured his wife on the dangers of taking medication
Answer: C
The passage says that "Jagan found his son's attraction to aspirin ominous. He merely replied, 'T'll get you better things to eat than this pill. Forget it, you understand?'"
Q18: How did Mali react when Jagan mentioned that people can die from poison?
A) He became frightened and stopped asking questions
B) He showed disinterest and changed the subject
C) He listened with interest, as if it was a story
D) He insisted on learning more about the dangers of poison
Answer: C
The passage states that when Jagan said "People die when they eat poison," Mali "listened with interest and asked, 'And then what?' as if listening toa story."
Q19: What was the significance of the "cool room" where Mali had his own space?
A) It was a secluded and quiet area for Mali to study
B) It was located close to the kitchen for easy access to food
C) It allowed Mali to observe the activities in the rest of the house
D) It was a well-ventilated and comfortable room for Mali to relax
Answer: C

The passage describes the "cool room" as a place where Mali "could enjoy privacy without losing sight of all the goings on in the house—such as the arguments between his father and mother or their conversation with visitors."
Q20: How did Jagan feel about his son Mali's growth and development?
A) He was indifferent and focused more on his work
B) He was concerned about Mali's safety and wellbeing
C) He was proud of Mali's height, weight, and physical growth
D) He worried about Mali's intellectual and academic progress
Answer: C

The text does not provide any information about Jagan's feelings towards Mali's intellectual or academic progress. However, it does state that Jagan was "very 'proud of his son's height, weight, and growth".
Q21: What was the significance of the "ancient pillar" mentioned in the passage?
A) It was a landmark in the family's ancestral home
B) It was a structural support for the house
C) It served as a gathering place for the family
D) It was a remnant of the original hut on the property
Answer: C
The passage describes the "ancient pillar in their courtyard" as the place where Jagan's wife "had knotted a towel around her temples and swayed madly back and forth".
Q22: What happened to the thatched hut that Jagan's father had initially lived in?
A) It was gradually expanded and transformed into the current house
B) It was demolished and the materials were reused for other purposes
C) It was preserved as a historical landmark on the family's property
D) It was abandoned and left to decay over time
Answer: B

The passage states that "When he found some money, he put up the walls of the bathroom, laying the bricks with his own hands, and that became practically the starting point of the house. They fetched water from a well across the road and stored it in old kerosene tins and drums. His father expanded the house from the back yard to the front. As a child, Jagan had no notion haw his father's fortune improved—although he heard vague words such as 'appeal,' 'lawyers,' 'lower court,' and 'upper court.'"
Q23: What was the purpose of the "margosa tree" in Jagan's backyard?
A) It provided shade and aesthetic value to the property
B) It was a source of firewood and building materials
C) It served as a perennial supply of twigs for tooth-brushing
D) It helped in the cultivation and growth of the coconut trees
Answer: C

The passage emphasizes Jagan's reliance on the margosa tree, stating that he "never ceased ta feel grateful to his father for planting a seedling in his tire and providing him with a perennial source of twigs—enough for his generation and the next".
Q24: How did the presence of the tall coconut tree near the bathroom affect the structure?
A) It provided natural cooling and ventilation
B) It caused damage to the corrugated roof with falling fronds
C) It made the bathroom feel more secluded and private
D) It added a scenic and tranquil ambiance to the area
Answer: B

The passage describes the coconut tree as "A very tall coconut tree loomed over the bath, shedding enormous withered fronds and other horticultural odds and ends on the corrugated roof with a resounding thud."

A) Nostalgic and reflective
B) Tense and conflict-ridden
C) Lighthearted and whimsical
D) Pragmatic and matter-of-fact
Answer: A
